opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've been something of a professional skeptic on this question for about fifteen years now, so you can probably guess where I'm going to come down.

Let me start with the theory, because I think that's where a lot of the confusion begins. Quantum annealing, or more generally the adiabatic algorithm, was proposed by Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and others around 2000. The idea is beautiful: you start in the easy-to-prepare ground state of some simple Hamiltonian, slowly deform it into a Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the answer to your optimization problem, and if you go slowly enough the adiabatic theorem says you'll end up at the answer. The catch is the phrase "slowly enough." How slow you need to go depends on the minimum spectral gap along the path, and for hard instances of NP-complete problems, that gap can become exponentially small. People showed fairly early on that there are instances where the adiabatic algorithm gets stuck in local optima, just like classical heuristics do, and needs exponential time. Nobody has any good reason to believe quantum annealing solves NP-complete problems efficiently in general. I'd say almost nobody in the field believes quantum computers can do that by any method.

There's also a nice theoretical point that tunneling, which was often the selling point, the idea that a quantum system can tunnel through a tall thin barrier where a classical simulated annealer would have to climb over it, does give you advantages on certain carefully constructed instances. But in many of those cases, it turned out that clever classical algorithms, like quantum Monte Carlo or other methods, could simulate what the annealer was doing with comparable efficiency. So the speedup was against a particular classical strawman, not against the best classical algorithm.

Then there's the experimental side, which was mostly about D-Wave. For years there were press releases claiming a quantum speedup of, you know, a hundred million times, and when you looked carefully, the comparison was against classical simulated annealing running on a single core, on problem instances tailor-made to suit the hardware. When people like Matthias Troyer and his collaborators did careful benchmarking, and when you compared against the best classical solvers, the speedup basically evaporated. I spent a lot of time on my blog in those years being the guy who said, "Wait, but compared to what?"

Now, to be fair, and I try to be fair, D-Wave's hardware did get better, and I think there's been genuinely interesting physics coming out of these devices, for example, using them as analog simulators of certain magnetic materials. Simulating quantum systems is, after all, the application where I'm most confident quantum computers will help. That's a different claim from "this will speed up your logistics or your portfolio optimization."

So where do I come out? I'd say that for generic optimization problems, the honest answer is that we don't have convincing evidence of any quantum speedup from annealing, and the theoretical expectation is that the speedup, if there is one, would be at most modest, maybe something Grover-like, which is quadratic, and possibly less, and which can easily get eaten by the overhead of error correction and the slow clock speeds of quantum hardware. It's possible that heuristic quantum optimization will turn out to win on some practically relevant class of instances. I don't rule that out. But the burden of proof is on the people making those claims, and the right way to meet it is careful comparisons against the best classical algorithms, not press releases.

If you want the place where I think quantum computing will really earn its keep, it's things like simulating chemistry and materials, and, for better or worse, Shor's algorithm breaking current public-key cryptography. Optimization is where the hype has been loudest and the evidence has been weakest.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is no convincing evidence of quantum speedup for generic optimization and that any speedup is expected to be at most modest, perhaps Grover-like (quadratic) or less, while leaving open possible wins on some practical classes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say my assessment has been pretty consistent for about fifteen years now, which is: skeptical, but with a careful account of why.

Let me separate two things. There's quantum annealing as an abstract algorithmic idea, and then there's the specific devices that companies like D-Wave have built. On the abstract side, the adiabatic algorithm is a perfectly legitimate quantum algorithm. We know it's universal in the sense that with the right Hamiltonians it can simulate any quantum circuit. And there are contrived examples where it provably beats classical simulated annealing, where you have a tall thin barrier and quantum tunneling gets you through where thermal hopping gets stuck. So the idea isn't crazy.

The problem is that for the optimization problems people actually care about, like scheduling or routing or anything NP-hard, nobody has ever shown an asymptotic speedup from annealing. And there are reasons to doubt there is one. You can also construct examples where annealing does exponentially worse than classical methods, because the spectral gap closes and you get stuck in a local minimum that the quantum dynamics can't escape in reasonable time. Generically, we have no theoretical reason to expect anything beyond, at best, a modest polynomial advantage, and for NP-hard problems in full generality we have strong evidence quantum computers can't give you exponential speedups at all.

Then on the hardware side, the story for years was that every time someone claimed a speedup for a D-Wave machine, a group of classical algorithms people would come along and match or beat it on a laptop. Sometimes within weeks. The devices have gotten better, and there have been more interesting recent claims about simulating quantum dynamics of magnets rather than solving optimization problems, which is actually a more plausible place to look for an advantage. But for optimization as such, I still don't think we've seen a convincing demonstration of a speedup that holds up against the best classical competition.

So my honest answer is: enormous uncertainty, no theoretical basis for the exponential claims you sometimes hear in marketing, and a long track record of classical methods catching up. If a real speedup shows up, I'd expect it to come from fault-tolerant gate-based machines running algorithms we can actually analyze, not from annealing.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about annealing speedups and says there is no demonstrated asymptotic speedup, but it does not state whether speedups beyond Grover’s square-root level are unknown for most optimization problems of interest.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between a speed-up that we can prove and one that we hope to see in practice. Quantum annealing is a way of trying to find a low-energy state of a system, where you’ve encoded the solution to an optimization problem in that state. The question is whether quantum effects help you get there faster than the best classical methods.

For certain specially constructed problems, we can show substantial advantages. But for the kinds of hard optimization problems people actually want to solve, we don’t have a general result saying that quantum annealing gives an exponential speed-up. In particular, there’s no good basis for saying it efficiently solves NP-hard problems in general.

People often invoke quantum tunneling: perhaps you can tunnel through a barrier where a classical algorithm has to climb over it. That’s a useful intuition, but it isn’t by itself a demonstration of a speed-up. The shape of the barrier matters, and classical algorithms have tricks beyond simply climbing over barriers.

So I’m open to useful advantages, but the case has to be made through careful comparisons with the best classical algorithms, looking at how performance scales as the problems get larger. That’s a much higher bar than showing that a quantum device beats one particular classical approach on a few examples.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no general result establishing an exponential speed-up for hard, practical optimization problems, but it does not address whether speed-ups beyond Grover’s square-root benchmark are known.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we don’t know yet. Quantum annealing is a physically interesting approach to optimization, but there’s no general result saying that it will solve hard optimization problems exponentially faster than classical algorithms.

The idea is to start a quantum system in an easy-to-prepare ground state and gradually change it so that its final ground state encodes the solution you want. The difficulty is that you might encounter an extremely small energy gap along the way. Then you may have to evolve the system extremely slowly, and whatever speed advantage you hoped for can disappear.

Quantum tunneling could help on certain kinds of optimization landscapes. But the relevant comparison is with the best classical algorithms, including algorithms designed specifically for those instances—not just with a straightforward implementation of simulated annealing. And you have to account for the overhead of encoding the problem in the hardware.

So I’m open to useful speed-ups for particular problems. What I’m skeptical of is the leap from ‘this device uses quantum effects’ to ‘therefore it efficiently solves NP-hard problems.’ That’s precisely the part that needs to be demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no general result showing exponential speedups for hard optimization problems, but it does not address whether quantum annealing can exceed a Grover-type square-root speedup for most problems of interest.
